chapter: Tick Chambers and the Dodds brothers
title: Advice on drinking, and young jazz players in Sweden and England
summary: He says non-drinkers die too, urges Dixieland players to keep it up, and describes European school bands.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Yeah, well you know people have that saying, if a fellow don't drink or don't smoke and he dies, the guy who the doctor tell him that he shouldn't drink, he'll tell you say, well, since the one never did drink and he died, you understand, so look at me, I'm still living and I'll drink. And eventually he might last a little longer, you know. That's right. So he just, so that's one thing I, I do recommend the boys who play Dixieland to keep it up, play the noise, because if they don't, just like I said in England in the interview, for us to hear jazz, we're going to have to go over there if we just keep it up, because all the youngsters over there, that's all they're doing. That's the majority. The kids don't take it up. The kids don't take it up. The little kids over there, ten, twelve years old, is playing jazz. That's young. That's young, that's right. Playing jazz. And them at sixteen is playing bands, they got bands. Even the school, we played a place in, yeah it was in Sweden. We played in Sweden, when the concert was over they had a school band who came there on the bus, you know, just like these college bands here. Played all the Dixieland tunes and all the spirituals and things. Out there in that snow playing it when we, after we, celebrating us after we came out the concert, after the concert was over. And I said now let's see how we are letting the things back, what they are, they calls it art. They love it.
